Consider a plate of mass $M$ that occupies the region $D$ in the upper half plane bounded by the polar circles $r=1,$ $r=2,$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above. The mass density at any point is proportional to the square of its distance from the origin. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the origin.

activity_context.topic_title: Moments of Inertia of Laminas About the Coordinate Axes

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14069995/assets/d1a19303937f1d515ca820516e10a73974b00f83884b05abb58dee49c81207f4.png)

Consider a plate of mass $M$ that occupies the region $D$ in the upper half plane bounded by the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16,$ shown above. Given that the mass is distributed uniformly across the plate, find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis.
feedback.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,\,0\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

The area of the plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2}=8\pi .
$$

 

Since the mass is distributed uniformly, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{8\pi }.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{M}{8\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{M}{8\pi }({\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{M}{8\pi }({\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{M}{8\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}{|}_{0}^{4}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\theta +\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{M}{8\pi }\cdot 64\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =4M.\end{aligned}
$$
